cards.explanation: The answer is: without passing judgment on his opinions. Verse 1 says, “Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions.” No clipboard, no pop quiz at the door. You open the door and let him in. I think plenty of people breathe easier hearing that.

The answer is False. Verse 2 says one person “…has faith to eat all things…” and the word weak goes to the other one, who “…eats only vegetables.” Paul doesn't call the eater of everything weak. Good thing, because I'd still be sulking if somebody had called me weak in my own bakery.

The answer is accepted. The verse ends with “…for God has accepted him.” That's the reason the one who doesn't eat everything must not judge the one who does. If God has already accepted him, who's left to hand out a rejection slip? Not me, friends.

The answer is master. Paul says, “To his own master he stands or falls.” His picture is a servant and his master, and the master is the one whose opinion counts. Everybody else in the room is just watching. Watching is a lot easier than being the boss, friends.

The answer is the Lord. Paul says, “And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” The servant's standing doesn't depend on whoever is judging him. It depends on the Lord. That's good news for anybody who's ever been sized up by somebody with a very strong opinion.

The answer is mind. Paul says, “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” He wants each person settled in his own thinking about the day he keeps. Convictions are meant to be walked out before the Lord, and not borrowed from the loudest voice around. Borrowing someone else's certainty is like wearing their apron: it never quite fits.

The answer is that they do it to the Lord. Paul says the one who keeps a special day, the one who eats and the one who abstains each do it “…to the Lord…” Three different choices, and the same direction. The thing they share is who they're doing it to.

The answer is True. Verse 6 says, “…he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.” So the one who skips certain foods is still thanking God. That's why this isn't a contest between the eaters and the skippers.

The answer is belong. Verse 8 says, “So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.” Notice it covers both living and dying. Nobody belongs to a rumor, a rule list or a cookie jar, friends. We belong to the Lord.

The answer is: to be Lord of both the dead and the living. Verse 9 says Christ died and returned to life “…that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.” That's a huge reach. It covers the people here now and the people already gone. Everybody Paul has been talking about already belongs to Him.

The answer is that we will all stand before God's judgment seat. Paul says, “For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat.” Notice the word all. That includes the person doing the judging. I think that tends to quiet the room fast.

The answer is himself. Verse 12 says, “So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.” Each person reports for himself. You don't turn in a report on somebody else's batch, friends. Mine is plenty to keep track of.

The answer is: not to put a stumbling block in a brother's way. Verse 13 says, “…make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way.” The energy that used to go into judging goes into keeping his path clear. Think of it like a hallway. Nobody wants to leave a box in the middle of it for someone else to trip over.

The answer is True. Paul says, “But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean.” He has just said he's convinced nothing is unclean in itself. Even so, he treats the other person's conviction with respect. That's the twist.

The answer is love. Paul says, “…you are no longer acting in love.” He's talking about what happens when your brother is distressed by what you eat. Love sets how you eat. Hunger doesn't, and neither does being right.
The answer is that Christ died for him. Paul says, “…your brother, for whom Christ died.” That's how much that brother matters. If Christ died for him, I'm not going to let a snack outrank him.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.” The kingdom isn't a menu. It's righteousness, peace and joy, and I'd say that's a better thing to chase.

The answer is: what leads to peace and builds each other up. Verse 19 says, “So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification.” Mutual edification means building each other up. It's a trade: you stop trying to win, and you start trying to build.

The answer is True. Paul says, “All food is clean, but it is wrong for a man to let his eating be a stumbling block.” He holds both halves together. The food is clean, and it is wrong to let eating be a stumbling block.

The answer is: eat meat or drink wine. Verse 21 says, “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.” The point is the brother. If it would cause him to stumble, you give it up.

The answer is condemn. Verse 22 says, “Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.” It's a blessing for the person whose conscience is clear about what he does. Most of us could use a clear conscience about the last cookie.

The answer is that his eating is not from faith. Verse 23 says, “But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith…” The problem isn't what's on the plate. He's doubting while he eats. That's the part Paul points to.
The answer is True. The last words of the chapter are, “…everything that is not from faith is sin.” It ends the chapter on faith. I think that's what holds the whole chapter together.
